findings.headline: Environmental property service projected to overspend by £400,000
findings.detail: The Property service under Head of Environmental and Neighbourhood Services has a budget of £230,076 for Period 1-4 but is already £103,913 over budget at month four. The service is projected to overspend by £400,000 for the full financial year 2026/27.
findings.matters: A £400,000 overspend on a £230,076 budget represents material cost control issues or unforeseen pressures. This scale of overspend will likely require reserve drawdown or additional borrowing, signaling financial management challenges that could affect the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Service budget to Period 4: £230,076; Budget remaining: £104,793; Period 4 variance: +£103,913; Estimated 2026/27 outturn: +£400,000 overspend

findings.headline: Large Covid-era reserve (£8.4m) still in reconciliation with unclear release timeline
findings.detail: The council holds £8.4m in Covid-19 funding relating to 2020/21 and 2021/22. This external reserve is not moving in 2026/27 but reconciliation and potential release is marked as in progress. Until resolved, this remains on the balance sheet but its ultimate destination is uncertain.
findings.matters: A £8.4m reserve held for an historical purpose creates balance sheet uncertainty; large releases or returns of unspent funding would materially impact the council's usable reserves position.
findings.figures: £8,439,412 held, no movement forecast in 2026/27
findings.quote: Balance of Covid-19 income and expenditure relating to 2020/21 and 2021/22. Reconciliation and return/release in progress.

findings.headline: Business Rates Equalisation Reserve being drawn to manage rate stress
findings.detail: The council forecasts drawing £325,000 from its business rate smoothing reserve for the remainder of 2026/27. This reserve exists to stabilise volatile business rate income. The drawdown suggests the council is forecasting business rate income below normal expectations.
findings.matters: Reliance on the smoothing reserve signals weaker business rate income than budgeted, which could reflect economic stress in the district or changing rateable values.
findings.figures: Opening £10,208,830, forecast movement -£325,000, ending £9,883,830
findings.quote: Funding to smooth the volatility of business rate income.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates £1m commitment for temporary restructuring staff
findings.detail: The council added £1m to its LGR internal capacity reserve in budget setting to fund temporary staff in Legal, Finance and Human Resources to handle additional workload. The forecast shows £1.124m will be drawn in 2026/27 to cover committed expenditure. A Cabinet report on the future structure is scheduled for October 2026.
findings.matters: This signals major structural change is imminent; the scale of temporary staffing costs indicates significant internal effort required for either merger, separation, or reorganisation, with uncertain duration.
findings.figures: £1m added in budget setting, forecast expenditure £1,124,279 in 2026/27, ending balance £609,196
findings.quote: To fund temporary staff to support the additional workload for internal support services including Legal, Finance and Human Resources. The forecast includes all committed expenditure.

findings.headline: Gateway site capital scheme requires £1.5m new reserve funding and commits £2.2m by year-end
findings.detail: The council has acquired a major development site (Gateway, Stratford-upon-Avon) in partnership with WMCA. It added £1.5m to reserves in budget setting specifically for NNDR costs and site clearance, bringing the total committed to £2.2m by 31 March 2027. A planning application for development has been submitted.
findings.matters: This is a material capital commitment with an external partner (WMCA); the council's obligations and timeline depend on the progress of planning approval and development, which carries execution risk.
findings.figures: Opening £970,980, MTFS addition £1,500,000, forecast balance 31 March £2,212,404
findings.quote: The Council has worked with the West Midlands Combined Authority to acquire the Gateway site located in Stratford-upon-Avon. This funding meets the Councils obligation under this agreement to cover the NNDR costs that may be due on the site until redevelopment. Additional funding was agreed as part of the budget setting process to clear the site, in order to progress the scheme.

findings.headline: Cost of Living Support reserve being completely depleted by year-end
findings.detail: The council forecasts spending £485,592 from this reserve over the year (having already spent £205,000 in the first four periods), drawing it to zero by 31 March 2027. The reserve was topped up with £250,000 in MTFS changes but that has proven insufficient.
findings.matters: Using reserves for one-off cost-of-living support is a temporary solution; if this need continues beyond March 2027, the council will have to fund it from revenue or accept further reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Opening £440,592, MTFS addition £250,000, movement -£205,000 (P1-4), forecast end balance £0
findings.quote: Grants to be issued for people needing additional support due to the cost of living crisis.

findings.headline: Inflation contingency reserve released entirely in budget setting
findings.detail: The council set aside £450,000 for unknown indexation across council contracts, but released it entirely in budget setting for 2026/27. This removes a key contingency for inflation pressures and suggests the council either needed the cash for other budget pressures or was confident of managing inflation within the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Removing an inflation contingency signals either budget pressure during planning, or reduced caution about inflation risk at a time when indexation remains uncertain.
findings.figures: £450,000 released, ending balance £0
findings.quote: This is for the unknown increase in indexation across all council contracts over and above what is held in the revenue contract inflation pot. This was released as part of the budget setting process for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget Monitoring Cabinet Report 7th Sept 2026 (Period 1-4) V2
findings.headline: Material non-domestic rate write-offs including fraud and government valuation error
findings.detail: Two significant NNDR write-offs totalling £137,853.50 are being approved: £26,495 for a property fraudulently entered on the rating list in 2023 (VOA unable to retrospectively remove liability), and £111,358.50 for a rateable value assessment error by the Valuation Office Agency.
findings.matters: Write-offs of this scale indicate collection control vulnerabilities and exposure to errors from government agencies, both creating revenue risk.
findings.quote: Account 1 £26,495 - This property was removed from the rating list in 2023. However, the Valuation Office Agency (VOA) is unable to retrospectively remove the liability for the 2021 and 2022 rating years. The property was originally entered into the list based on a lease that was fraudulently signed.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget Monitoring Cabinet Report 7th Sept 2026 (Period 1-4) V2
findings.headline: Council tax collection costs rising £35,000 due to debt recovery and discount administration
findings.detail: Council Tax shows an unfavourable variance of £35,000 at estimated outturn driven by increased costs associated with debt collection and recovery, plus professional fees for a review of the single person discount scheme.
findings.matters: Rising debt collection and administration costs suggest either deteriorating collection rates or increased administration burden, both reducing net council tax income.
findings.figures: £35,000 unfavourable variance
findings.quote: Council Tax shows an unfavourable variance of £35,000, due to costs associated with debt collection and the recovery of those costs, in addition to professional fees associated with reviewing the single person discount.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget Monitoring Cabinet Report 7th Sept 2026 (Period 1-4) V2
findings.headline: Housing benefits persistently under-recovering subsidy and overpayments
findings.detail: Housing Benefits shows unfavourable variances of £138,589 at Period 4 and £30,000 at estimated outturn, specifically due to under-recovery of housing benefit overpayments and shortfall in housing benefit subsidy from central government.
findings.matters: Recurring shortfalls in housing benefit recovery indicate either rising overpayments (welfare trend) or inadequate central subsidy, both of which create structural budget pressure.
findings.figures: £138,589 at Period 4; £30,000 at outturn
findings.quote: Housing Benefits shows an unfavourable variance of £138,589, due to under-recovery of housing benefit overpayments and a shortfall in housing benefit subsidy.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget Monitoring Cabinet Report 7th Sept 2026 (Period 1-4) V2
findings.headline: Building safety maintenance commitments at Elizabeth House requiring reserve funding
findings.detail: Building Services shows an unfavourable variance of £229,265 at Period 4, mainly for building safety maintenance commitments at Elizabeth House to be funded from earmarked reserves. A further £46,000 unfavourable outturn is forecast for increased NDR, utilities, and building security costs.
findings.matters: Unexpected or escalating building safety costs at a specific property may signal deferred maintenance or emerging compliance issues with the estate.
findings.figures: £229,265 at Period 4; £46,000 at outturn
findings.quote: Building Services shows an unfavourable variance of £229,265, mainly due to building safety maintenance commitments in relation to Elizabeth House to be funded from earmarked reserves.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget Monitoring Cabinet Report 7th Sept 2026 (Period 1-4) V2
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves used to fund current operational expenditure across multiple service areas
findings.detail: At Period 4, the council was using £1,095,919 of earmarked reserves to fund current operational costs in employee expenses, supplies and services, and third-party payments, recorded as a 'favourable' variance on recharges to other accounts.
findings.matters: Using designated reserves for routine service delivery suggests the council cannot cover normal operations from revenue and is consuming reserves to balance the budget, indicating structural pressure.
findings.figures: £1,095,919 at Period 4
findings.quote: Recharges to Other Accounts shows a favourable variance of £1,087,658, which mainly relates to the use of earmarked reserves totalling £1,095,919 at Period 4. This is mainly funding expenditure within Employee, Supplies and Services and Third-Party Payments.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget Monitoring Cabinet Report 7th Sept 2026 (Period 1-4) V2
findings.headline: New public convenience cleaning contract creating £400,000 cost overrun
findings.detail: Property services show an unfavourable variance of £400,000 at estimated outturn, specifically attributed to increased public convenience cleaning costs following the new cleaning contract. This represents a structural increase in ongoing operational costs.
findings.matters: A £400,000 cost overrun on a single service contract indicates budget-setting failure or unbudgeted scope change, both of which signal governance or forward-planning risks.
findings.figures: £400,000 unfavourable variance
findings.quote: Property shows an unfavourable variance of £400,000, due to increased public convenience cleaning costs, following the new cleaning contract.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget Monitoring Cabinet Report 7th Sept 2026 (Period 1-4) V2
findings.headline: General reserves forecast to decline by 33%, from £20.6m to £13.9m
findings.detail: The general reserve account is expected to fall from £20,640,526 at 1 April 2026 to £13,853,283 by 31 March 2027. This £6.8 million reduction is driven by a planned £1.2m contribution, £3.2m earmarked reserves funding, and £2.5m revenue slippage, partially offset by the year-end favourable position.
findings.matters: A 33% reduction in general reserves in a single year materially constrains financial flexibility and resilience against unexpected pressures or investment needs.
findings.figures: Opening £20,640,526; closing £13,853,283; net transfer from reserves £6,946,243
findings.quote: Opening Balance 1 April 2026 20,640,526 ... Estimated Revenue Reserve 31 March 2027 13,853,283

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 7 September 26 Capital Budget Monitoring P1- 4 2026-27
findings.headline: £10.4 million in capital projects rolled forward from 2025/26 constitutes three-quarters of the total 2026/27 capital budget
findings.detail: The capital budget originally agreed for 2026/27 in February 2026 was £3.372m. Slippage from 2025/26 adds £10.386m, bringing the total capital expenditure budget to £13.944m. This means the majority of the current year's capital spending will be devoted to completing projects originally planned for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Slippage on this scale signals either constraints in project delivery or compressed timescales. A finance director would need to understand why prior-year projects didn't complete; a lender would view this as a possible indicator of resource, planning, or capability constraints affecting capital delivery reliability.
findings.figures: 2026/27 base budget £3,372,000; slippage £10,386,479; total budget £13,944,321
findings.quote: The Cabinet 6 July 2026 Slippage of 2025/26 items. 10,386,479

findings.headline: £3.5m housing acquisition scheme for temporary accommodation is fully committed but shows no actual expenditure four months into financial year
findings.detail: The council has committed the full £3.5m for acquisition of housing to rent for temporary accommodation provision, but the spending table records no actual expenditure in April–May 2026-27.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a material cost pressure for many councils. A fully-committed but unexecuted £3.5m scheme this far into the year may indicate procurement delays, financing complications, or that the commitment timing differs from budget assumptions.
findings.figures: £3.5m committed; £0 actual April–May 2026-27
findings.quote: Acquisition of Housing to Rent 1,000,000 2,500,000 3,500,000 3,500,000

findings.headline: Evesham Place fit-out project overran budget by £14,700 due to project management fees not included in original estimate
findings.detail: The project was budgeted at £55,024 but actual spend reached £58,680 in the first four months. Narrative indicates project management fees were originally expected to be delivered in-house but were subsequently added to the capital budget.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on straightforward fit-out work suggest inadequate initial scoping and budgeting discipline. This pattern on multiple schemes indicates potential cost control issues across the capital programme.
findings.figures: Budget £55,024; actual spend £58,680; overspend £14,700
findings.quote: Original budget did not include PM fees as due to be in-house. This was agreed to be funded from Project Implementation Budget.

findings.headline: Leisure centre solar panel scheme shows cost growth and extended delivery timeline due to unexpected roof works at Southam
findings.detail: The Stratford and Shipston leisure centre solar panel works funded by Sports England Lottery grant are complete, but the Southam works (funded by Climate Change Reserve) have been postponed to summer 2027 after discovery of additional roof remediation works. The scheme is already £23,169 over budget.
findings.matters: Cost growth on externally-funded energy schemes affects their return on investment and suggests the council encountered unforeseen structural issues. Extended timelines delay energy savings and may indicate wider condition issues in the council's estate.
findings.figures: Budget £395,950; overspend £23,169; works postponed to summer 2027
findings.quote: Southam works postponed to summer 2027 as additional roof works are required.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation will dissolve the council as a district authority and merge it into a unitary on 1 April 2028, with explicit concerns about retaining financial reporting capacity.
findings.detail: Stratford will cease to exist as a district in a Warwickshire local government merger. Government announcement expected July 2026, Structural Changes Order late 2026, elections May 2027, vesting 1 April 2028. The council is managing transition planning with external support (PwC), but explicitly flags the challenge of retaining expertise to deliver the final accounts with an unmodified opinion in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Structural dissolution creates operational uncertainty and staff turnover risk. The s151 officer's explicit concern about capacity to complete the 2027/28 accounts signals the transition may strain the council's financial reporting function.
findings.figures: Vesting day 1 April 2028; Structural Changes Order expected late 2026 to early 2027; elections May 2027
findings.quote: Careful planning will be essential as we approach vesting day to ensure the Council retains the expertise and capacity required to achieve full assurance and deliver the 2027/28 Statement of Accounts with an unmodified opinion.

findings.headline: Council has lost five-year housing land supply after new NPPF methodology doubled housing need; now has only 2.74 years.
findings.detail: A December 2024 NPPF change increased the district's calculated housing need from 553 to 1,126 dwellings per annum. In June 2025 the council showed 5.06 years of supply, but a September 2025 planning appeal reduced this to 2.74 years. This renders much of the Core Strategy (adopted 2016, intended to guide development to 2031) out-of-date and triggers numerous speculative applications the council did not plan for.
findings.matters: Loss of planning control affects the council's ability to shape development, its leverage in section 106 negotiations, and revenue certainty from planning obligations. The council has had to redirect resources mid-year to address this.
findings.figures: Housing need doubled from 553 to 1,126 dwellings per annum; land supply fell from 5.06 years to 2.74 years
findings.quote: This has a significant impact on the determination of planning applications for residential development, requiring the presumption in favour of sustainable development to be applied in reaching planning decisions. It has also prompted the submission of a large number of speculative planning applications outside of the current policy framework.

findings.headline: Council receiving disclaimed opinions on audited accounts for three consecutive years; will persist until 2027/28.
findings.detail: Brought forward balances from 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25 carry disclaimed audit opinions, part of a nationwide backlog where nearly 1,000 councils had outstanding statements by end of 2024. While in-year transactions are audited, the council's opening position and accumulated reserves cannot be independently verified. Assurance will be rebuilt over several audit cycles to 2027/28.
findings.matters: Unverified opening balances limit a lender's ability to assess the council's actual financial position and reserve adequacy for the years under consideration.
findings.figures: Nearly 1,000 statements outstanding across English councils by end of 2024; backstop dates extend to 2027/28
findings.quote: Like many other local authorities, this has left the Council with disclaimed opinions for these years. It is essential that as much work can be undertaken in the future years audits to build back the assurance that the missing audits has created.

findings.headline: Housing Benefits income shortfall of £137,721 at Period 2 due to subsidy and overpayment recovery issues
findings.detail: Housing Benefits shows a £137,721 unfavourable variance at Period 2, attributed to under-recovery of housing benefit overpayments and a shortfall in housing benefit subsidy from government. This variance does not clearly appear in the estimated full-year outturn projections in Section 6, making it unclear whether the issue is expected to resolve or is absorbed into other lines.
findings.matters: Benefits subsidy volatility and poor overpayment recovery directly reduce council income. Income shortfalls of this scale indicate either reduced subsidy allocation or administrative efficiency issues in overpayment chasing.
findings.figures: Period 2 variance: £137,721 unfavourable
findings.quote: Housing Benefits shows an unfavourable variance of £137,721, due to under-recovery of housing benefit overpayments and a shortfall in housing benefit subsidy.

findings.headline: Unplanned preventative building safety and maintenance works at Elizabeth House generating cost pressures
findings.detail: Building Services shows an unfavourable variance of £35,832 at Period 2 and an estimated £40,000 for the full year, primarily due to additional Non-Domestic Rates costs and preventative building safety maintenance works at Elizabeth House. This is unbudgeted expenditure triggered by building safety maintenance requirements.
findings.matters: Preventative safety maintenance works indicate building condition or compliance issues that were not in the original budget. This suggests potential for further unbudgeted expenditure if building issues expand, and may indicate deferred maintenance elsewhere.
findings.figures: Period 2 variance: £35,832 unfavourable; estimated full-year outturn: £40,000 unfavourable
findings.quote: Building Services shows an unfavourable variance of £35,832, mainly due to additional NDR costs and preventative building safety maintenance works in relation to Elizabeth House.

findings.headline: Council drawing down £4.2m from general reserves in a single year, reducing financial buffer by 20%
findings.detail: The council is using a net transfer of £4,194,504 from reserves to balance the 2026/27 revenue position, combined with £3,200,000 drawn from earmarked reserves to fund specific commitments. This reduces the general reserve balance from £20,640,526 (opening) to £16,446,022 (estimated year-end)—a 20% reduction in the council's financial buffer in a single year.
findings.matters: Large single-year reserve drawdown materially reduces the council's capacity to absorb unexpected demands or income shortfalls, and indicates the council is dependent on reserves to balance the in-year revenue account rather than living within its tax/fee income.
findings.figures: Opening general reserve: £20,640,526; estimated closing: £16,446,022; net transfer to revenue: £4,194,504; earmarked reserves drawn: £3,200,000
findings.quote: This, together with a net transfer from reserves of £4,194,504 leaves revenue reserves with an estimated balance of £16,446,022 as at 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: HEART disabled adaptations scheme demand exceeding budget mid-year; statutory duty funding shortfall requiring additional £300,000
findings.detail: The budget for the HEART adaptation scheme (£1,194,592) is fully committed by Period 2. The council is requesting an additional £300,000 to continue meeting its statutory duty to provide adaptations. To manage this, the council will pause any discretionary adaptations above the £30,000 statutory threshold for the remainder of 2026/27. This follows a pattern: in 2025/26, the initial budget also required government top-up (£83,896) and Cabinet approval for an additional £250,000.
findings.matters: Sustained demand for adaptations is forcing the council to request mid-year funding adjustments and pause non-statutory work. This signals both sustained high need and budgeting shortfalls, indicating the initial budget does not reflect actual demand patterns.
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget: £1,194,592 fully committed; additional request: £300,000. 2025/26: government top-up £83,896 plus Cabinet-approved addition £250,000
findings.quote: In order for the Council to continue to meet its statutory duty, an additional £300,000 is required in year – this will be ringfenced to meeting the Council's statutory duty. Any discretionary adaptations or funding above the £30,000 statutory threshold will be paused for the remainder of 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 6 Jul 26 Capital Outturn Slippage P1-12 2025-26
findings.headline: Council holds £15.95m in S.106 developer contributions and £4.03m in CIL funds—significant contingent spending liabilities
findings.detail: The council holds £15.95m in S.106 (section 106 planning obligations) with £1.27m already committed, and £4.03m in Community Infrastructure Levy funds with £2.10m committed and £1.92m unallocated. These represent contractual obligations to spend funds per planning agreements within specified timeframes.
findings.matters: These are not discretionary funds; they are committed to be spent by deadlines set in planning conditions. Slow capital execution creates clawback risk if councils cannot deliver projects on time
findings.figures: S.106 total held £15.95m (committed £1.27m); CIL total £4.03m (committed £2.10m, unallocated £1.92m)
findings.quote: Total S.106 funds held amount to £15.95m (including committed funds of £1.27m and after expenditure of £313k). Total unspent CIL funds amount to £4.03m, (including committed funds of £2.10m), unallocated CIL funds held for future allocation total £1.92m.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 6 Jul 26 Capital Outturn Slippage P1-12 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital delivery massively behind plan—only £2.27m of £13.7m budget spent, with £10.4m carried into 2026/27
findings.detail: The council budgeted £13.7m for capital projects in 2025/26 (including £4.9m brought forward from prior years). Actual spending was only £2.27m—a 16% outturn—with the majority of projects delayed. The council now requests £10.4m carry-forward into 2026/27, indicating systematic delivery challenges across capital schemes.
findings.matters: Persistent under-spending on capital budgets signals project management or execution risk, raising questions about the council's ability to deliver its capital strategy on schedule
findings.figures: Budget £13,722,694; actual expenditure £2,270,855; slippage requested £10,386,479
findings.quote: the total Capital Expenditure Budget for the current year, including S.106, plus other additions, and slippage, as outlined in the 2024/25 Capital Budget Outturn Report, now totals £13,722,694. Actual expenditure for the period to 31 March 2026 totalling £2,270,855

findings.headline: £640k investment interest gain masks underlying cost pressures and depends on rates staying high
findings.detail: The outturn shows a favorable position of £639,881 on Investment Interest, attributed to 'increased interest rates than budgeted, sums invested and therefore additional interest receipts'. This single line item makes up most of the year's overall favorable position of £513k. The gain is entirely dependent on interest rate levels and the council's investment holdings remaining elevated.
findings.matters: If interest rates fall or the council is forced to draw down investments to fund other commitments, this gain will evaporate. The council's apparent financial health is fragile: underlying operations showed multiple cost overruns that were masked only by an interest-rate windfall.
findings.figures: £639,881 investment interest gain; £513,492 total favorable position
findings.quote: increased interest rates than budgeted, sums invested and therefore additional interest receipts

findings.headline: Housing benefits overpayment recovery and council tax enforcement both underperforming
findings.detail: Housing Benefits recorded an unfavorable variance of £52,679 due to 'under-recovery of housing benefit overpayments and a shortfall in housing benefit subsidy'. Council Tax recorded £144,228 unfavorable due to 'shortfall in the recovery of court costs'. Both are income-collection shortfalls, not one-off absences.
findings.matters: Persistent shortfalls in collection of housing benefit overpayments and council tax court costs suggest reduced collection capacity or rising arrears. Both are core revenue streams. If collection continues to underperform, the council will face cash flow pressure.
findings.figures: Housing Benefits £52,679 shortfall; Council Tax recovery £144,228 shortfall
findings.quote: under-recovery of housing benefit overpayments and a shortfall in housing benefit subsidy... shortfall in the recovery of court costs

findings.headline: Contractor inflation now outrunning budget assumptions, signalling cost pressure ahead
findings.detail: The Corporate Budget recorded an unfavorable variance of £198,735, explicitly driven by 'higher than budgeted contractor inflation' and lower vacancy savings. This is a forward indicator: if contractors are already exceeding budget in 2025/26, forecasts for future years need upward revision.
findings.matters: Contractor cost overruns reduce headroom for discretionary spending and capital projects. If inflation is not contained, the council may be forced to defer capital schemes or cut service provision.
findings.figures: Corporate Budget £198,735 unfavorable; contractor inflation cited as a driver
findings.quote: reduction in vacant posts resulting in lower than budgeted vacancy savings and higher than budgeted contractor inflation

findings.headline: Audit working papers of mixed quality—management unable to provide adequate evidence without rework
findings.detail: Auditors noted that working papers provided by management were of mixed quality and required multiple rounds of clarification and rework. Examples included receiving unsupported spreadsheets as evidence and difficulties obtaining transactional-level reports needed to complete audit testing. This delayed audit work substantially. Management and auditors have agreed to hold a debrief meeting to improve the process for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Poor quality financial records and working paper support indicate underlying issues in the finance function's competence, systems, or resourcing. Weak internal controls over record-keeping increase the risk of undetected errors in the financial statements and suggest the Council lacks financial management discipline.
findings.figures: Working paper quality rated AMBER (developing); finance team accessibility rated GREEN; auditors noted this was expected given no full audit since 2020/21
findings.quote: Working papers received were of mixed quality. We experienced some occasions of needing to go back to management to clarify what we needed and to ensure that the quality of the working papers was appropriate.

findings.headline: £880k error identified in property valuations—right-of-use asset incorrectly reversed, left uncorrected
findings.detail: Auditors identified an error in property accounting where a transaction relating to right-of-use assets was incorrectly reversed in the financial statements. The error would increase property, plant and equipment by £880k and reduce the revaluation reserve by £880k if corrected. Although classified as immaterial (below the £1.44m materiality threshold), auditors left the error unadjusted in the published accounts, indicating a control failure in the asset accounting process.
findings.matters: Errors in asset valuations directly affect balance sheet accuracy and the reserves position reported to lenders. Even errors classified as non-material indicate potential for larger undetected errors and suggest the finance function's quality control systems are ineffective.
findings.figures: Error value: £880k; overall materiality: £1.44m; performance materiality: £0.866m; trivial threshold: £72.2k
findings.quote: This resulted in a non-material error being identified, which remains unadjusted within the financial statements. The impact of correcting this error would be to reduce the revaluation reserve and increase the value of PPE by £880k.

findings.headline: Financial statements issued 49 days late due to IFRS 16 complications—missed 1 July statutory deadline
findings.detail: The Council failed to meet the statutory deadline of 1 July 2025 for issuing unaudited financial statements, instead issuing them on 19 August 2025. The two-month delay was directly attributed to complications with implementing IFRS 16 lease accounting. The subsequent statutory public inspection period (19 August to 29 September) was compressed as a result, limiting time for public scrutiny.
findings.matters: Late financial reporting indicates control weaknesses in the finance function and reduces transparency to stakeholders and lenders about the Council's year-end position. Delayed accounts also delay the audit cycle and any identification of problems.
findings.figures: Statutory deadline: 1 July 2025; actual issue: 19 August 2025 (49 days late); public inspection period: 19 August to 29 September 2025
findings.quote: The Council issued their unaudited financial statements on 19 August 2025 due to IFRS16 application complications.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting implementation incomplete—management failed to value lease assets and liabilities
findings.detail: Management has not completed the required valuation work for IFRS 16 implementation, which mandates recognition of right-of-use assets and lease liabilities on the balance sheet. Auditors identified that management undertook no work to calculate the opening and closing valuations of these material balance sheet items, making it impossible to audit completeness or accuracy of lease accounting disclosures. This directly contributed to the disclaimer of opinion.
findings.matters: Incomplete lease accounting implementation reveals gaps in the finance function's technical accounting capability. Lease assets represent material balance sheet items affecting reported financial position. This suggests potential for other complex accounting—pension valuations, property revaluations—to also be incorrect.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 identified as high inherent risk area in audit plan; right-of-use asset and lease liabilities valuations remain unadjusted
findings.quote: Management has not undertaken appropriate work to calculate the opening and closing valuation of the right of use asset and liabilities.

findings.headline: Auditors disclaim opinion on 2024/25 accounts—fourth consecutive year without audit assurance
findings.detail: Azets has disclaimed their audit opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, unable to obtain sufficient work to support an unmodified opinion before the 27 February 2026 backstop date. Following disclaimed opinions in 2021/22, 2022/23, and 2023/24, the Council now has four consecutive years without audit assurance. The disclaimer prevents the auditors from confirming accuracy of opening balances, key accounting estimates including pension valuations and lease accounting, and management override testing.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on audited financial statements to assess financial position and repayment capacity. Four consecutive years without an audit opinion means the Council's actual financial position cannot be independently verified, creating material uncertainty for anyone extending credit.
findings.figures: Four consecutive disclaimed years (2021/22 to 2024/25); materiality £1.44m; backstop date 27 February 2026; build-back plan extends to 2027/28
findings.quote: The audit opinions in the Council's financial statements for 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24 were all disclaimed.

findings.headline: Transitional Protection grant funding peaks in 2028/29 at £2.855m then falls sharply to £1m, creating a known future pressure.
findings.detail: The council is receiving temporary Transitional Protection funding introduced by the Government to cushion the impact of the Fair Funding Review. This support rises from £744k in 2026/27 to £2.855m in 2028/29, then drops back to £1m in 2029/30 and remains at £1m. This is explicitly temporary support, and the sharp reduction in year 4 will require the council to absorb a £1.855m loss of government support.
findings.matters: Transitional support is a known cliff-edge. The council's budget plan currently assumes this support continues, but Government policy is to phase it out. If the council has not built alternative savings into the 2029/30 budget, it will face a sudden £1.8m+ shortfall.
findings.quote: A new Adjustment Support Grant has been introduced to ensure no authority would be worse off in 2026/27 and £115m of new funding has been identified to fund this as part of the transitional protection arrangements.

findings.headline: The S151 officer describes the five-year budget as 'challenging but deliverable', signalling tight financial management.
findings.detail: Section 3.2.3 states the balanced budget "remains challenging but deliverable" in the Statutory Officer's assessment. This is measured language for significant delivery risk: the budget is not comfortable, it requires execution against plan with little room for variance.
findings.matters: An S151 officer's assessment of challenge indicates the council's finance team expect the budget to be difficult to deliver. This leaves little room for service demand spikes, pay awards beyond plan, or one-off costs.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The budget presented is a balanced budget over the five year period. In the view of the Statutory Officer to the Council, it remains challenging but deliverable.

findings.headline: General Fund Reserves will decline from £16.9m to £3.6m over five years, with the council drawing down reserves every single year to balance the budget.
findings.detail: The council is drawing £4.4m from reserves in 2026/27 to balance the budget, with further draws of £1.5m–£3.1m in each subsequent year through 2030/31. While the S151 officer confirms reserves will remain above the £3.0m minimum threshold, the trajectory is steep: a 79% reduction in working reserves over five years.
findings.matters: Reserves exist to absorb shocks (pay disruption, service demand spikes, inflation). A council in sustained drawdown has limited buffer. When reserves are being used to fund recurring expenditure every year, not just one-off pressures, it signals the base budget is structurally unaffordable.
findings.figures: Reserves 1 April 2026: £16.932m; reserves 31 March 2031: £3.618m. Annual drawdowns: £4.420m, £1.535m, £1.549m, £3.090m, £2.720m
findings.quote: the Council use £4.4m of General Fund Reserves in order to fund expenditure. The reserves will then continue to be utilised to support the Council's budget in the period 2027/28 to 2030/31.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility income has collapsed: £420,000 shortfall in 2025/26 and budget cut to £800,000 for 2026/27 with no future provision.
findings.detail: The council's budget for the current year has been hit by a £420,000 funding shortfall from reduced EPR payments (waste packaging fees shared with producers). The 2026/27 budget responds by cutting the EPR income line to £800,000, and the budget removes EPR income entirely from 2027/28 onwards, signalling this income source is no longer reliable.
findings.matters: A council losing a material recurring income stream without a replacement is a structural budget pressure. For a lender, unexplained income loss signals either reduced economic activity in the area or a change in the scheme terms that the council cannot control.
findings.figures: £420,000 shortfall in 2025/26; income budget cut to £800,000 in 2026/27; zero provision from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: The estimated outturn position for 2025/26 has been updated to reflect a £420,000 funding shortfall arising from reduced Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) payments.

findings.headline: Council relying on 'internal borrowing' (reserve drawdowns) to fund capital, with no external borrowing planned
findings.detail: The council states it has no external debt and plans no external borrowing over the medium term. Instead, it funds capital using 'internal borrowing'—drawing down reserves held on the balance sheet. This practice is expected to continue. The negative capital reserve figures in the financing table show reserves being depleted year-on-year.
findings.matters: Persistent reserve drawdown to fund capital is unsustainable and signals that ongoing capital spending or revenue deficits are being masked by reserve depletion. Once reserves are exhausted, the council will face service cuts or forced borrowing.
findings.quote: At the end of 2024/25, the Council had no external borrowing, using the cash in its balance sheet arising from reserves to fund 'internal' borrowing. It is expected that this element of 'internal' borrowing will continue over the medium term.

findings.headline: Commercial investment income target may require review due to government settlement uncertainty
findings.detail: The council has set a 'modest' income target from commercial activities within the MTFS. However, it explicitly flags that this target may need revision depending on year-on-year government settlement outcomes. This contingency language suggests the target may not be achievable or is subject to unpredictable political change.
findings.matters: Uncertainty over a stated income stream undermines budget assumptions. If commercial income falls short, the council faces a revenue gap and may need to draw additional reserves or cut services.
findings.figures: Described as 'modest' with no specific figure disclosed
findings.quote: The Council currently has a modest income target within the current MTFS from investment in commercial activities. Pending the outcome of year-on-year government settlement, the income target may need to be reviewed.

findings.headline: Planned capital spending exceeds identified funding sources, creating an unresolved financing gap
findings.detail: The capital financing table shows planned expenditure with total finance available plus borrowing (which is zero) leaving a cumulative shortfall of £743k–£250k per year. This gap between planned spending and available/borrowed funds is unexplained and suggests either optimistic budget assumptions or reliance on undisclosed reserve drawdowns.
findings.matters: An unmatched financing gap indicates either overly ambitious capital planning, concealed reliance on reserves, or delayed delivery. This affects the credibility of the capital plan and signals reserve depletion risk.
findings.figures: Net of Funding & Borrowing shortfalls: (£743k) 2024/25, (£90k) 2025/26, (£250k) 2026/27–2028/29
findings.quote: The Capital Investment Programme can be funded from the following sources: Government Grants & Other Contributions… Capital Receipts… Section 106 Contributions… Revenue Contributions… Capital Expenditure Reserves… Borrowing

findings.headline: Capital programme contracting by 70% from 2025/26 to 2026/27, falling from £11.6m to £3.4m
findings.detail: Total planned capital expenditure drops dramatically from £11.6m in 2025/26 to £3.4m in 2026/27, and continues declining to £961k by 2028/29. This sharp contraction suggests either severe budget constraints or inability to progress planned schemes.
findings.matters: A 70% year-on-year cut to the capital programme signals financial stress, reduced investment capacity, or slippage in major projects. This impacts the council's ability to maintain and improve assets.
findings.quote: Capital Investment is the term used to cover all expenditure by the Council that can be classified as capital under legislation and proper accounting practice.

findings.headline: Right to Buy sharing agreement ending in 2026, eliminating a material capital funding source
findings.detail: The council has relied on post-transfer Right to Buy receipts from the 1999 housing stock sale to South Warwickshire Housing Association. This income stream, one of the listed capital funding sources, is coming to an end. The council notes that capital receipts from RTB sales will decline significantly once this agreement terminates.
findings.matters: Loss of this recurring capital income (£734k in 2024/25) removes a source of financial flexibility and forces greater reliance on alternative funding or asset sales.
findings.quote: the final receipts will be received in 2026. In addition the Council holds a limited number of land interests and has a programme to release sale proceeds from these assets to support the Revenue Account.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation added as new corporate risk linked to financial sustainability and staff retention
findings.detail: Following announcements about local government reorganisation, the Council has added a new corporate risk to its register. The report indicates this risk intersects with existing financial sustainability risks and staff retention risks, suggesting potential impacts across multiple critical areas of council operations.
findings.matters: Reorganisation could materially affect the council's financial position, borrowing requirements, staffing capability, and service delivery—factors material to both lenders assessing creditworthiness and council finance directors planning operations.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided in this cover report
findings.quote: Following announcements surrounding local government reorganisation a new corporate risk has been included on this subject. This risk is also referred to within the financial sustainability risk and staff retention risk.
